summary: Updates the Diameter base protocol (RFC 3588) so a realm can advertise which Diameter applications each of its servers supports, using an extended S-NAPTR service tag in DNS. Without this, a peer would have to try each server in turn until one supports what it needs.

eli5.summary: A big office has many phone lines, and each person handles different topics. This lets the office post a directory saying who handles what, so callers do not have to ring everyone.

questions: how does diameter peer discovery work
subtitle: Lets a realm advertise, in DNS, which Diameter applications and transports each server supports.

tldr.problem: The Diameter base protocol lets a realm advertise nodes and transports in DNS, but not which Diameter applications they support, so a peer might have to run a capability exchange with every node until it finds a suitable one.
tldr.mechanism: An extended S-NAPTR service tag of the form aaa+ap followed by the Application Identifier, with an optional transport protocol tag, lets a NAPTR record say exactly which application and transport a server offers.
tldr.outcome: A client can pick the right server from DNS alone. The RFC updates RFC 3588 and asks DNS administrators to keep legacy records too.

facts.label: Service tag
facts.value: aaa+ap followed by the Application ID

today: RFC 6408 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3588. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Diameter base protocol (RFC 3588) defines three mechanisms for peer discovery. One is a NAPTR query for a server in a given realm, which maps a domain to an SRV record or A/AAAA record for contacting a server over a particular transport.

That mapping cannot say which Diameter applications a node supports. This RFC builds on the Straightforward-NAPTR (S-NAPTR) DDDS application of RFC 3958 and defines service and protocol tags so that a peer supporting a specific application and transport can be discovered. It updates Section 5.2 of RFC 3588.
sections.eli5: The old directory said where the offices were, but not what each office did. The new one adds the topic.

sections.title: The Extended Service Field
sections.content:
The RFC refines the S-NAPTR ABNF with two new tag forms.

  • Application service: aaa+ap followed by an appln-id of 1 to 10 digits, the Diameter Application Identifier written as a decimal integer without leading zeros. The identifier is a 32-bit unsigned integer allocated by IANA.
  • Application protocol: diameter. followed by tcp, sctp or tls.tcp.

For example, aaa+ap6:diameter.sctp means the node supports the Diameter SIP application (6) over SCTP. For a vendor-specific case, aaa+ap16777251:diameter.sctp means the 3GPP S6a application over SCTP.

Querying applications MUST NOT parse the protocol tags. The dot is only for readability and implies no structure. The tags are unrelated to the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry. The NAPTR service field is at most 256 octets, including a one-octet length field.
sections.eli5: Each record gets a short label like a name tag: the topic number, then how to reach the office. The label is read as a whole, not taken apart.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
DNS administrators SHOULD also provision legacy NAPTR records in the RFC 3588 style, so peers that only follow RFC 3588 still work. When both kinds exist, the extended S-NAPTR records MUST have higher priority than the legacy ones, for example through a lower order or preference value.

Every IETF Standards Track Diameter application MUST be associated with an aaa-service tag, and a Diameter agent MUST be able to use the extended tag to find an agent for such applications.
sections.eli5: Keep the old signs up for visitors who only read those, but put the new, more detailed signs first.

sections.title: Peer Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
The querying node must know the realm and the Application Identifier it wants. The realm could come from the Network Access Identifier in the User-Name AVP or from the Destination-Realm AVP. This RFC replaces the NAPTR query steps of RFC 3588 Section 5.2 with the following, depending on what the returned service fields look like.

  • aaa+apX:Y: the realm supports the extended format. If X is the needed application and Y a supported transport, resolve the replacement field. Otherwise abandon discovery.
  • aaa+apX: if X is the needed application, resolve it and try all supported transports in the order given in Section 2.1 of RFC 3588. Otherwise abandon discovery.
  • aaa:X: Diameter is supported without the extended format. If X is a supported transport, resolve the replacement field.
  • aaa: likewise legacy, try all supported transports.
  • No NAPTR-based discovery at all: move on to the next mechanism in RFC 3588.

The RFC's example realm ex1.example.com publishes records for NASREQ (ID 1) and Credit Control (ID 4) over SCTP, and an SRV lookup of _diameter._sctp.ex1.example.com returns two servers on port 3868.

Diameter is peer-to-peer, but many applications behave as client and server, and the role is not advertised in NAPTR tags or in capability exchange. Such discovery should therefore only be used by a client to find servers.
sections.eli5: The visitor reads each sign. If it names the right topic and a way they can travel, they go there. If not, they give up on this directory and try another way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA reserved aaa for Diameter in the S-NAPTR Application Service Tag registry of RFC 3958, plus tags for existing IETF applications.

  • aaa+ap1 NASREQ, aaa+ap2 Mobile IPv4, aaa+ap3 Base Accounting, aaa+ap4 Credit Control, aaa+ap5 EAP, aaa+ap6 SIP, aaa+ap7 Mobile IPv6 IKE, aaa+ap8 Mobile IPv6 Auth, aaa+ap9 QoS, and aaa+ap4294967295 Relay.
  • Four 3GPP tags (STa, S6a, SWm and S9) and ten WiMAX Forum tags.
  • Protocol tags diameter.tcp, diameter.sctp and diameter.tls.tcp.

Future IETF Diameter applications MUST reserve their tag. Vendor-specific application IDs are allocated First Come First Served, but the tag registry requires a specification that is an RFC of any category, so such an application needing this functionality MUST have an RFC reserving its tag.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of topic numbers and travel methods, and new ones have to be added to it properly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The change is based on S-NAPTR, a simplification of NAPTR, so the security considerations of RFC 3588 apply and no extra mechanisms are needed. The RFC adds one caution: a malicious host doing S-NAPTR queries learns the applications supported by a realm's Diameter agents faster, which could help it pick targets if some applications have known vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: A public directory also helps a troublemaker find the right door faster.

data.title: Credit Control over SCTP
data.code:
;;        order pref flags service   regexp replacement
IN NAPTR  50    50   "s"   "aaa+ap4:diameter.sctp" ""
             _diameter._sctp.ex1.example.com
